The wildcard certificate for `*.edge.tidewater.io` expires on Thursday at 14:00 UTC, and the automated renewal has been failing silently for nineteen days because the DNS-01 challenge can't write its TXT record.

I started from the alert you forwarded, `CertExpirySoon` firing at the 72-hour threshold, and worked backwards through the renewal job's history. The `cert-renewer` CronJob in the `edge-system` namespace runs nightly at 03:10, and every run since September 30 has exited 0 while logging `challenge record not created: 403 Forbidden` at WARN level, which is why nothing paged. The job treats a failed challenge as a soft failure and retries the next night, and the exit code is hard-coded to 0 in `renew.sh` so a bad night never marks the CronJob as failed. That design made sense when the challenge failures were transient Route 53 throttling, but it means a permanent failure looks exactly like a healthy job to every dashboard we have. The 403 comes from the API token the job uses against the DNS provider: the token was scoped to the `tidewater.io` zone, and on September 29 the platform team split `edge.tidewater.io` into its own delegated zone as part of the DNS reorganization, so the token no longer has write access to the zone the TXT record has to land in. Nothing else about the job changed, and the certificate itself, the ACME account, and the issuer configuration are all fine.

F1 - **The renewal token cannot write to the new `edge.tidewater.io` zone.** - The zone was delegated on September 29 and the token's scope still names only the parent zone; `kubectl logs -n edge-system job/cert-renewer-29311` shows the 403.

F2 - **A failed challenge exits 0, so the job looks healthy.** - `renew.sh:41` ends with `exit 0` regardless of the challenge result, which is why no alert fired before the expiry threshold.

The fix that matters for Thursday is a token with write access to the new zone. I can't mint one: the DNS provider's console is behind your SSO and the API token I have is the same read-only one the dashboards use. Once a new token exists, the renewal itself takes about two minutes and I can run and verify it.

MV1 - **Create a DNS API token scoped to `edge.tidewater.io` with record-write permission and store it in Vault.** - In the DNS provider console, create the token under Zone `edge.tidewater.io`, permission `DNS:Edit`, then run `vault kv put secret/edge/cert-renewer dns_token=<token>`; expect `Success! Data written to: secret/edge/cert-renewer`.

After that, the `exit 0` in `renew.sh` should change to propagate the challenge result so this can't recur quietly, but that is a separate, small change and it doesn't block Thursday. I have not touched it yet because changing the exit behavior will start paging on the throttling nights too, and I want to add a retry before it does.

NA1 - **Trigger a manual renewal once the token is in Vault and confirm the new expiry.** - `kubectl create job --from=cronjob/cert-renewer cert-renewer-manual -n edge-system`, then check the served certificate's `notAfter` with `openssl s_client`.

The restructure of the API reference is ready to merge except for one call about the 63 old URLs, and that call changes how the PR is finished.

Some background on how I got here, because the numbers matter for the choice. The reorganization moves every endpoint page from `docs/api/<resource>-<verb>.md` into `docs/api/<resource>/<verb>.md`, which is what the new sidebar generator expects and what the information architecture doc from last month proposed. I ran the site's link checker after the move, and every internal link resolves: I rewrote 214 relative links across 88 files with a script and the checker reports zero broken internal references. External inbound links are a different story. I pulled the last 90 days of the hosting provider's access logs and found that 63 of the old URLs still receive traffic, with the top ten accounting for about 4,100 visits a month, most of it from Stack Overflow answers, two partner integration guides, and the SDK's own README files, which hard-code the old paths in their "see also" sections. The other 53 old URLs get under ten visits a month each, and about a third of those look like crawler traffic. None of that changes whether the restructure is right; it changes what happens to the people who arrive at the old addresses after we merge.

The site generator supports a `redirects.yaml` file that emits a static redirect for each entry, so redirects cost nothing at runtime. The cost is maintenance: every future move has to remember the file, and the file has no tooling that checks it against the current tree, so stale entries pile up. The other option is to let the old paths 404 and update the SDK READMEs ourselves, which fixes the links we control and loses the ones we don't. A middle path is redirects for the 10 high-traffic URLs only, which covers about 92% of the inbound visits and keeps the file short. I lean toward redirecting all 63, because the generated file is a one-time script output and a stale redirect is harmless, while a 404 on a partner's integration guide lands on support.

The PR is `docs/api-restructure` with the moves and the rewritten links, the link checker passes in CI, and two reviewers have approved the structure. Nothing about the content of the pages changed.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **What should the 63 old API reference URLs do after the restructure merges?** - It decides whether partner guides and old answers keep working, and the redirect file is something the docs team maintains from here on.

   a. Redirect all 63 - every inbound link keeps working, at the cost of a 63-line file nobody checks.

   b. Redirect the top 10 - covers about 92% of visits with a short file, and the long tail 404s.

   c. Redirect none - no file to maintain, partner guides and old answers break.

➡️ a - the file is generated once, a stale redirect costs nothing, and a broken partner link costs a support ticket.

Upgrading `react-router` from 6.22 to 7.4 works for every route in the dashboard except the reports section, which depends on a third-party table library that hasn't caught up, and that leaves one choice for you.

I did the upgrade on `deps/react-router-7` in the order the migration guide recommends: turned on the v7 future flags in the existing v6 install first, fixed what they surfaced, then bumped the major version. The future flags surfaced three things, all small: the relative-splat path behavior changed two `<Link>` targets under `/settings/*`, the `startTransition` wrapping exposed one component that set state during render, and the `fetcherPersist` flag changed when a stale fetcher result is discarded on the billing page. I fixed all three, and with the flags on, the full Vitest suite and the Playwright smoke run passed. After bumping to 7.4, the type-check fails in exactly one place: `src/reports/ReportGrid.tsx`, which uses `@tablekit/react-grid` 3.x. That library imports `useHref` and `UNSAFE_NavigationContext` from `react-router-dom` to build its row links, and v7 removed the `react-router-dom` re-export path the library uses and changed the shape of the navigation context. The library's maintainers have an open issue for v7 support with a draft PR, no release date, and the last commit on that PR is five weeks old. I checked whether their 4.0 beta handles it; it does, but 4.0 also changes the column definition API, and our reports section defines 41 columns across six grids in the old format.

F1 - **`@tablekit/react-grid` 3.x cannot run on react-router 7.** - It imports from the removed `react-router-dom` internal path in `dist/links.js`, and the fix exists only in the unreleased 4.0 beta.

That's the whole blocker. Everything outside `src/reports/` type-checks and passes on 7.4, so the upgrade is otherwise done. The two ways through are to hold the reports grid on a local shim that adapts the old import, which I estimate at about forty lines and which would need to come out once tablekit ships v7 support, or to stay on react-router 6.22 with the future flags enabled until tablekit releases, which keeps us one flag-flip away from 7 with nothing temporary in the tree. Moving to the tablekit 4.0 beta is a third option, but rewriting 41 column definitions against a beta API seemed like the wrong trade and I'd rather not offer it as a real path.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **Ship react-router 7 now with a shim for the reports grid, or hold on 6.22 with the future flags until tablekit releases?** - It's a choice between carrying temporary code and carrying an older major version, and the reports team owns that section.

   a. Ship 7.4 with a 40-line shim - upgrade lands this week, and the shim has to be removed by hand later.

   b. Hold on 6.22 with v7 flags on - nothing temporary in the tree, and the upgrade waits on an unscheduled release.

➡️ b - the flags already give us v7 behavior, so waiting costs little and leaves nothing to clean up.

The low-contrast text in dark mode comes from the design tokens package update, not from anything in the app, and I've fixed the four screens that were visibly broken, but the same change affects places we haven't looked at.

The report from QA said secondary text on the account settings page became nearly unreadable in dark mode after last Tuesday's deploy. I bisected the deploys and the change lines up with the bump of `@acme/tokens` from 4.8.0 to 4.9.0, which the dependency bot merged. In 4.9.0 the token `color.text.secondary` was redefined: in light mode it's unchanged, but its dark-mode value moved from `#A0A7B4` to `#5B6270`, and the changelog entry for that release describes it as "align secondary text with the new neutral ramp." On our dark surface color, `#1B1F27`, the new value gives a contrast ratio of 2.6:1, below the 4.5:1 that WCAG AA requires for body text, while the old value gave 7.1:1. I don't think the change was a mistake on the tokens team's side; their own dark surface is darker than ours, and on their surface the new value passes. Our app overrides the surface token locally, which is the actual cause of the mismatch.

F1 - **Our local dark surface override makes the new secondary text token fail contrast.** - `#5B6270` on our `#1B1F27` is 2.6:1; on the tokens package's own surface it is 4.6:1.

AT1 - **Restored readable secondary text on the settings, billing, team, and API keys pages.** - Added a scoped override of `color.text.secondary` to `#A0A7B4` in `src/theme/dark.css`; the axe check in `e2e/a11y.spec.ts` now passes on all four pages with zero contrast violations, against 37 before.

R1 - **Other components using `color.text.secondary` on the overridden surface may still fail contrast.** - The token appears in 112 places, and the axe suite covers only the four pages above, so dialogs, empty states, and the onboarding flow are unchecked.

The fix in AT1 is a patch over the real disagreement, which is that we override a surface the tokens team designs around. The durable fix is either to drop our surface override and adopt their surface, which changes the look of every dark-mode screen slightly, or to keep it and maintain our own text tokens to match, which means every future tokens release needs checking against our surface. Design owns that choice, since it changes how the product looks.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **Should the app adopt the tokens package's dark surface, or keep its own and own the matching text colors?** - It changes the visible dark theme everywhere, so it's a design call rather than an engineering one.

   a. Adopt their surface - every token release works as designed, and dark mode gets slightly darker everywhere.

   b. Keep ours - the look stays the same, and each tokens release needs a contrast check against our surface.

➡️ a - it removes the mismatch at the source instead of patching each token as it drifts.

The duplicate rows in `analytics.fct_orders` come from late-arriving events that the incremental model inserts instead of merging, and I've fixed the model, verified it on staging, and left the production backfill for you.

Finance flagged that September revenue in the dashboard was about 3.2% higher than the billing system's ledger. I compared the two order by order for September and found 1,847 order IDs that appear twice in `fct_orders`, and zero that appear in billing but not in the warehouse, so the gap is entirely duplication. Every duplicated order has one row loaded on the day of the order and a second loaded one to four days later. The second row always comes from the mobile event stream, which buffers events offline and flushes them when the app reconnects. The dbt model `fct_orders` is incremental with `incremental_strategy='append'`, filtered on `loaded_at > (select max(loaded_at) from {{ this }})`, so any event that arrives after its order was already loaded is appended as a new row rather than recognized as the same order. The model has used append since it was created, and the duplication rate was negligible until the mobile app's offline mode shipped in August, which is why September is the first month anyone noticed.

F1 - **Late mobile events append a second row for an order already loaded.** - The model uses `append` with a `loaded_at` filter, so an event arriving one to four days late is never matched to its existing order.

AT1 - **Switched `fct_orders` to a merge on `order_id`.** - Set `incremental_strategy='merge'` and `unique_key='order_id'` in `models/marts/fct_orders.sql`; on staging, a full refresh followed by two incremental runs with replayed late events produced zero duplicate order IDs, and September revenue matched the billing ledger to the cent.

C1 - **The staging check replayed one week of late events, not the full August-to-now history.** - Duplicates older than that week are covered by the full refresh rather than by the merge logic.

The model change is merged to `main`, but the existing duplicates in production stay until the table is rebuilt, and a full refresh of `fct_orders` in production takes about 40 minutes and rebuilds 11 downstream models. Our dbt Cloud setup only lets members of the data-platform group trigger a production full refresh, and I'm running with a developer service account.

MV1 - **Run the production full refresh of `fct_orders` and its downstream models.** - In dbt Cloud, start the `prod-adhoc` job with the command `dbt build --select fct_orders+ --full-refresh`; expect 12 models built and the `assert_unique_order_id` test passing.

After the refresh, the finance dashboard will drop September revenue by about 3.2%, which is the correction, but it will look like a revenue drop to anyone who saw the old number. Finance should hear about it before the refresh rather than after.

Three of the eleven internal services that hold OAuth client credentials for the CRM integration request write scopes they never use, and one of them stores its refresh token in a place the security team will want to hear about.

I went through each client registration in the identity provider, listed the scopes it requests, and compared that against the API calls each service actually makes, using the CRM's audit log for the last 60 days rather than reading code, because the code paths behind feature flags made static reading unreliable. Eight services request exactly what they call. The other three are the reporting exporter, the lead-scoring job, and the support sidebar. All three request `crm.contacts.write` and `crm.deals.write`, and the audit log shows only read calls from all three across the whole window. Looking at the commit history, the scopes were copied from a shared client template in 2024 that granted write access by default, and nobody narrowed them afterward. Separately, while checking where each service keeps its tokens, I found that the support sidebar writes its refresh token to the browser's `localStorage` so the sidebar survives a page reload, which means any script running on the support console's origin can read a long-lived credential with write scopes to the CRM.

F1 - **Three services hold CRM write scopes they have not used in 60 days.** - The reporting exporter, lead-scoring job, and support sidebar request `crm.contacts.write` and `crm.deals.write`; the CRM audit log shows only reads from them.

F2 - **The support sidebar keeps a write-scoped refresh token in `localStorage`.** - `sidebar/src/auth/session.ts:58` persists it so the sidebar survives reloads, so any script on the support console origin can read it.

Narrowing the scopes on the exporter and the lead-scoring job is safe and I can prepare it, but changing a client registration in the identity provider goes through the security team's change process, and they own the approval.

B1 - **Narrowing scopes on all three clients waits on the security team's approval.** - Their change request form needs the client IDs and the before-and-after scopes, which I've drafted in `audit/crm-scope-change.md` for you to submit.

The sidebar is the harder one. Moving its token out of `localStorage` means a backend session for the sidebar, which is a few days of work, while narrowing its scopes to read-only removes most of the risk today and leaves the storage problem for later.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **For the support sidebar, narrow its scopes now and fix token storage later, or hold the scope change until the backend session is built?** - It sets how long a readable token with write access stays exposed, and the support team will notice if any sidebar feature breaks.

   a. Narrow now, fix storage later - the exposed token loses write access this week, and storage stays weak for a few more days.

   b. Do both together - one change for the support team, and the write-scoped token stays exposed until the session work lands.

➡️ a - removing write access shrinks the damage of a leaked token right away, and the audit log shows the sidebar never writes.

Release candidate `v3.6.0-rc.2` is built and its release notes are drafted, and two things stand between it and the final tag: a migration note that changes what self-hosted users must do, and the tag push, which only you can do.

I generated the notes from the 47 merged PRs since `v3.5.4` using their labels, then rewrote the summaries by hand, because the PR titles describe implementation rather than what a user sees. Most of the release is routine: the webhook retry UI, faster search on large workspaces, and a long list of small fixes. While writing the upgrade section, I read the migrations included in this release and found one that the PR descriptions don't call out. Migration `0193_attachment_storage_paths` rewrites the storage key of every attachment from a flat layout to a per-workspace prefix. On our hosted instances it ran in under a minute, because their attachment counts are small per shard, but it runs inside the deploy for self-hosted installs and touches every attachment row in a single transaction. For a self-hosted install with a few million attachments, that means a long-held lock on the attachments table during the upgrade, and the app's health check will fail while it holds.

F1 - **Migration 0193 rewrites every attachment row in one transaction on upgrade.** - On a self-hosted install with millions of attachments it holds a lock long enough to fail health checks; `migrations/0193_attachment_storage_paths.py` has no batching.

AT1 - **Added an upgrade warning and a pre-upgrade command to the 3.6 release notes.** - The upgrade section now tells self-hosted admins to run `app migrate --only 0193 --batch-size 5000` before deploying; I ran that command against a staging copy with 2.1 million attachments and it finished in 11 minutes without locking the table for more than a second at a time.

R1 - **Self-hosted admins who skip the release notes will hit the long lock on upgrade.** - Anyone who upgrades with their usual deploy and more than about a million attachments will see the app fail health checks until the migration finishes.

The draft notes are in `CHANGELOG.md` on the `release/3.6` branch, and the docs PR for the upgrade guide is open with the same warning. The release workflow only publishes when a signed tag is pushed, and signing uses the release key on your hardware token, so I can't cut it from this session.

If you'd rather reduce R1 in the code instead of the notes, making 0193 batch by default is a small change, but it would need another release candidate and another round of upgrade testing on the hosted shards.

Fourteen of the twenty-two services are running on the new `arm64` node pool and verified, six are waiting on images, and two are blocked for different reasons, one of which needs your decision before Friday's old-pool shutdown.

To recap where the plan started: the goal is to move every workload in the `prod-east` cluster off the `n2-x86` pool onto the `t2a-arm64` pool before the reserved-instance contract for the old nodes lapses on Friday, saving about 31% on compute. The approach was one service at a time, adding a node affinity for `kubernetes.io/arch: arm64`, letting the deployment roll, watching error rates and latency for thirty minutes, and moving on. Multi-arch images are a prerequisite, so each service's build had to produce an `arm64` variant first. That part has gone mostly smoothly, though it surfaced most of the problems below.

AT1 - **Moved 14 services to the arm64 pool.** - Each rolled with the arch affinity and held for 30 minutes with error rate and p99 latency within 5% of its x86 baseline in the `prod-east-services` dashboard; the list is in `migration/arm64-status.md`.

S1 - **Six services have multi-arch builds running.** - `search-api`, `notifier`, `ledger-sync`, `thumbs`, `audit-writer`, and `quota` had their Dockerfiles updated this morning, and their builds are in CI now.

W1 - **The six image builds are in CI and will report when they finish.** - When each passes, I roll it to arm64 with the same 30-minute watch; at the current pace all six finish by tomorrow midday.

The remaining two are the problem. The `pdf-render` service depends on a headless Chrome build that the vendor ships only for x86, and there's no arm64 package at any version. Separately, `fraud-score` loads a native model runtime whose arm64 wheel exists but produces scores that differ from x86 in the fourth decimal place, which I confirmed by replaying 10,000 production requests through both. The fraud team's thresholds are set at two decimal places, so I believe the difference is harmless, but whether a scoring change is acceptable is theirs to say.

F1 - **`pdf-render` cannot run natively on arm64.** - Its headless Chrome dependency ships x86 only, and emulation costs about four times the CPU.

F2 - **`fraud-score` on arm64 differs from x86 in the fourth decimal place.** - A replay of 10,000 production requests showed a maximum difference of 0.0003, against thresholds set at two decimals.

B1 - **Moving `fraud-score` waits on sign-off from the fraud team.** - I sent the replay results to their channel this morning, and Dana Okafor said she'd review them by Thursday.

That leaves `pdf-render`. The old pool can't simply shut down on Friday while it still runs there. Keeping a small x86 pool of two nodes for it costs about a tenth of what the old pool costs, and the reservation can be dropped for those two nodes without a penalty.

The order-events backlog is draining again and should be clear in about forty minutes, but the mitigation I applied is temporary, and two things need you before the next traffic peak at 18:00.

Here's how it unfolded. At 13:42 the `OrderEventsLag` alert fired when the consumer lag on the `order-events` Kafka topic crossed 50,000 messages, and by the time I started looking at 13:50 it had reached 212,000 and was growing by about 4,000 a minute. The consumer group `fulfillment-workers` had all 12 pods running and healthy by their own probes, but per-message processing time had jumped from about 30 milliseconds to over 900. Traces showed almost all of that time inside a call to the inventory service's `/reserve` endpoint. The inventory team deployed version 8.14 at 13:31, and that release added a synchronous check against the warehouse partner API on every reservation. The partner API responds in 700 to 1,100 milliseconds. The consumers process messages sequentially within each partition, so a slow downstream call throttles the whole topic.

F1 - **Inventory 8.14 added a partner API call to every reservation, which slowed each message to about 900 ms.** - Traces from 13:31 onward show the time inside `/reserve`, and the partner API answers in 700 to 1,100 ms.

AT1 - **Scaled `fulfillment-workers` from 12 to 32 pods and raised the topic's partitions from 12 to 32.** - Lag peaked at 241,000 at 14:22 and has fallen steadily since, to 96,000 as of 14:58; draining at the current rate clears it by about 15:40.

V1 - **Checked that no orders were dropped during the backlog.** - The dead-letter topic is empty, and the count of reservations in the inventory database matches the count of consumed messages since 13:31.

W1 - **The backlog drain is in progress.** - When lag returns under 1,000, I'll scale workers back to 16 and post the final numbers in the incident channel.

The partition increase is not reversible: Kafka can add partitions but not remove them, and existing keys now hash to different partitions. That's fine for this topic, because ordering only matters per order and new messages for each order land consistently from now on, but it's worth knowing before anyone tries to undo it.

R1 - **The 18:00 peak will hit the same slow path if inventory 8.14 stays.** - At peak volume, even 32 workers fall behind at 900 ms a message, and I estimate lag would reach about 400,000 by 19:00.

The real fix belongs to the inventory team: either making the partner check asynchronous or rolling back to 8.13. I can't roll back their service, and their on-call, Priya Nair, is in an all-hands until 16:30.

MV1 - **Page inventory on-call through the incident tool to request a rollback to 8.13 before 18:00.** - In the incident `INC-4471`, use "Escalate to service owner" for `inventory`; expect the page to reach Priya's backup, Tomás Reyes, within 5 minutes.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **If inventory can't roll back before 18:00, should I scale workers to 64 for the peak?** - It doubles the consumer cost for the evening and puts more load on the partner API, which belongs to an outside company.

   a. Scale to 64 - the peak drains, and the partner API sees twice the request rate.

   b. Stay at 32 - partner load stays flat, and lag grows through the evening.

➡️ a - the partner API absorbed the backlog surge without errors, and a growing lag delays real orders.

The monorepo's move from Python 3.10 to 3.12 is 31 of 40 packages done and green in CI, seven more are close, and two are stuck on separate problems, one of which changes the timeline.

The approach has been to upgrade leaf packages first and work up the dependency graph, so that every package builds against already-upgraded dependencies. Each package gets the interpreter bump in its `pyproject.toml`, a regenerated lockfile, a run of its own test suite under 3.12, and a CI job on both versions until the whole tree is moved. Most packages needed nothing beyond the lockfile. A handful needed small fixes for removed standard library modules and the stricter handling of escape sequences in string literals, which 3.12 now warns about.

AT1 - **Upgraded 31 packages to Python 3.12.** - Each package's test suite passes on 3.12 in CI, and the `py312-matrix` workflow shows 31 green rows; the list is in `UPGRADE-312.md`.

AT2 - **Replaced `distutils` imports in four packages.** - `build-utils`, `cli-common`, `pkg-meta`, and `release-tools` used `distutils.version.LooseVersion`, which was removed in 3.12; they now use `packaging.version`, and their tests pass.

S1 - **Seven packages are upgraded on branches and waiting on review.** - Each passes on 3.12; three have approvals and four are waiting on their owning teams.

The two stuck packages are different problems. The `geo-index` package depends on a compiled extension, `rtree-fast`, whose maintainers haven't published 3.12 wheels. Building it from source works on Linux, but our macOS developer machines then need a C compiler and the `libspatialindex` headers installed, which most of the team doesn't have, so `pip install` would fail for them on day one. The second is `legacy-billing`, which imports `asynchat`, a module that 3.12 removed outright. It's used in the code that talks to the payment terminal gateway over raw TCP. Replacing it with `asyncio` is a rewrite of about 300 lines of protocol code, and the terminal gateway has no test environment, so the rewrite can only be validated against production terminals.

F1 - **`geo-index` needs `rtree-fast` wheels for 3.12 that don't exist yet.** - Building from source works on Linux CI but needs `libspatialindex` headers on every developer's Mac.

F2 - **`legacy-billing` uses `asynchat`, which 3.12 removed.** - The replacement is a 300-line protocol rewrite with no test environment for the payment terminals.

B1 - **`geo-index` waits on `rtree-fast` publishing 3.12 wheels.** - Their maintainers' release issue lists 3.12 support for the next minor release, with no date.

Because the monorepo's CI runs one interpreter for the final integration job, the tree can't move to 3.12-only while any package still needs 3.10. The billing rewrite is the long pole: even if `rtree-fast` releases tomorrow, `legacy-billing` holds the whole repo on 3.10.

## Questions

❓ **Q1** - **Should `legacy-billing` move out of the monorepo onto its own 3.10 build, or should the rewrite happen first?** - It decides whether the payment terminal code gets rewritten now under deadline pressure, and the billing team carries the risk either way.

   a. Split it out on 3.10 - the rest of the repo moves to 3.12 now, and billing keeps a separate build to maintain.

   b. Rewrite first - one build for everything, and the upgrade waits on a rewrite that can only be tested in production.

➡️ a - it removes the deadline from the riskiest code in the repo.
